findings.headline: The Financial Recovery Silver and Gold Groups were replaced by a Financial Recovery Board during 2025/26.
findings.detail: The Financial Recovery Board meets fortnightly to consider progress against savings and other actions in the plan. Quarterly reporting continues through the finance monitoring report to Cabinet and Overview and Scrutiny Committee.
findings.matters: A change in the body that oversees financial recovery is a governance change that other councils with recovery plans may recognise and compare.
findings.figures: Financial Recovery Board meets fortnightly
findings.quote: However, the impact of the Financial Recovery Silver & Gold Groups has been somewhat limited, leading to them being replaced by the new Financial Recovery Board during 2025/26.

findings.headline: KPMG's 2025/26 value for money work identifies 4 significant risks, which translate into 2 significant weaknesses.
findings.detail: The auditor notes that the four weaknesses are all consistent with its prior-year findings, and that no significant weaknesses have been raised over any new areas. It reserves the right to raise weaknesses linked to imminent Housing Regulator and CQC reports.
findings.matters: A council with two significant weaknesses in value for money is the same position a peer or lender would need to understand before relying on the council's governance.
findings.figures: 4 significant risks; 2 significant weaknesses; 4 weaknesses in total, all consistent with prior year
findings.quote: 4 significant risks identified, which currently translate into 2 significant weaknesses

findings.headline: The forecast cumulative schools deficit at Q1 2026/27 is £7.7m, up from £4.1m for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The number of schools in deficit also continues to rise, according to the auditor's review of the Q1 2026/27 update.
findings.matters: A rising schools deficit sits on top of a council's own financial position in the way the paper describes for high needs funding across England.
findings.figures: Forecast cumulative schools deficit £7.7m at Q1 2026/27; £4.1m for 2025/26
findings.quote: The number of schools in deficit also continues to rise, with a forecast full-year cumulative deficit of £7.7m as at Q1 vs a full-year cumulative deficit of £4.1m for 2025/26.

findings.headline: A risk linked to the North London Waste Authority's new Energy Recovery Facility has been given the top score of 25 on the Risk Register.
findings.detail: The auditor says persistent delays and increasing costs threaten the viability of the project and could increase the future levy charged to the council.
findings.matters: A top-scored risk on a shared waste project is an exposure that other boroughs in the same authority will also carry.
findings.figures: Risk score of 25 (top score)
findings.quote: There is an emerging risk – which has now been assigned a top score of 25 on the Risk Register

findings.headline: The North London Waste Authority levy for 2026/27 rose 7.1% to £12.1m, and is forecast to rise 14.3% to £13.5m in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 levy was £11.3m. The auditor says there remains significant uncertainty over how actual costs will align to the MTFS, because the operational start for the new Energy Recovery Facility is unclear.
findings.matters: Waste disposal levies are a fixed cost that councils can't easily reduce, and the new incinerator delay is a shared exposure for all seven north London boroughs.
findings.quote: we are aware through review of the 2026/27 budget process that this has increased again year on year by 7.1%, to £12.1m.

findings.headline: Year-end cash was £116.1m, against £23.2m a year earlier, which the paper attributes to timing of payments and receipts.
findings.detail: The paper says the increase is primarily due to timing differences in payments and receipts rather than a positive change in the council's financial health. Gross debt compared with the capital financing requirement rose from 0.70:1 to 0.78:1.
findings.matters: A lender reading the balance sheet needs to know that a large year-end cash balance reflects timing rather than underlying financial strength.
findings.quote: It should be noted that the increase in the cash position is primarily due to timing differences in payments & receipts rather than a positive change in respect of the Council’s financial health.

findings.headline: The CIPFA resilience index 2025 gives Haringey a particularly high score on reserves, interest payable and gross debt.
findings.detail: The index is based on 2024/25 data. The auditor also notes a worsening score on social care as a proportion of overall expenditure.
findings.matters: Peers and lenders use the CIPFA index to compare councils' financial risk, so a high score on the same measures used by others is directly comparable.
findings.figures: CIPFA resilience index 2025, based on 2024/25 data
findings.quote: Haringey has a particularly high score in terms of the lack of reserves, reduction in reserves, interest payable per net expenditure and gross debt

findings.headline: Housing Demand including Temporary Accommodation was the largest 2025/26 overspend at £7.0m, ahead of Finance & Resources at £4.7m and Children's at £1.7m.
findings.detail: Adults delivered a £1.5m surplus on budget, so the largest overspends have changed since 2024/25. The Temporary Accommodation overspend is on top of £10.7m of cost pressures already built into the 2025/26 budget.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are a common pressure across English councils, and the scale of overspend against a budget that already included a large allowance is useful for peers to compare.
findings.figures: Housing Demand including Temporary Accommodation £7.0m; Finance & Resources £4.7m; Children's £1.7m; Adults surplus £1.5m; £10.7m built into budget for Temporary Accommodation pressures
findings.quote: These are now Housing Demand including Temporary Accommodation (£7.0m), Finance & Resources (£4.7m, primarily linked to strategic property overspend) and then Children’s (£1.7m).

findings.headline: The 2026/27 savings target of £23.2m includes £8.3m of new schemes not already approved in previous years.
findings.detail: The auditor notes that the £23.2m target is a reduction from the 2025/26 target, despite the worsening financial position, and would be greater than any gross delivery in the previous four financial years.
findings.matters: A savings target that exceeds recent delivery and includes only a small amount of new schemes is the specific gap the auditor's statutory recommendation addresses.
findings.figures: £23.2m 2026/27 savings target; £8.3m new schemes; 2025/26 target £29.3m
findings.quote: Of this £23.2m, only £8.3m related to new schemes identified as part of this budgetary process that were not already approved in previous years.

findings.headline: Q1 2026/27 forecasts 77% savings achievement, with £4.9m of the target forecast as non-deliverable.
findings.detail: Of the £4.9m non-deliverable, £4.0m is cross-cutting savings. The auditor says this is a recurring theme from 2025/26 findings.
findings.matters: Forecast non-delivery of cross-cutting savings in a second consecutive year is the same pattern that the auditor has raised as a statutory matter.
findings.figures: 77% savings achievement forecast; £4.9m non-deliverable; £4.0m of which cross-cutting
findings.quote: This overspend also includes an expected achievement of only 77% of the savings target, with £4.9m of the target being forecast as non-deliverable, of which £4.0m represents cross-cutting savings.

findings.headline: Q1 2026/27 forecasts a full-year overspend of £21.7m, after £84.3m of EFS.
findings.detail: Without EFS, the cumulative budget shortfall is £106.0m. The auditor says the speed at which the 2026/27 budget has deteriorated confirms that the budget-setting weakness remains.
findings.matters: A budget that is overspending in the first quarter, even after government support, is the clearest signal of whether the recovery plan is working.
findings.figures: £21.7m forecast overspend; £84.3m EFS; £106.0m cumulative shortfall without EFS
findings.quote: We note that as at Q1 2026/27 the Council is forecasting a full-year overspend of £21.7m, which is after accounting for £84.3m of EFS

findings.headline: The 2026/27 General Fund budget of £353.0m was approved with an £84.3m shortfall, to be met by EFS.
findings.detail: Full Council approved the 2026/27 budget and the 2026/31 MTFS on 2 March 2026. MHCLG approved EFS of up to £84.3m for 2026/27 on 23 February 2026.
findings.matters: A budget approved with a gap of this size, funded by government capitalisation, is the central fact of the council's financial sustainability position, and peers will be watching the same route.
findings.figures: £353.0m General Fund budget; £84.3m shortfall; £84.3m EFS approved
findings.quote: identified a shortfall of £84.3m between planned income and expenditure.

findings.headline: Each £1m of EFS adds £83,000 a year to revenue costs for 20 years, at current rates.
findings.detail: The auditor says the annual cost of continuing to rely on EFS would be £8.8m if the 2026/27 cumulative budget shortfall of £106.0m is accurate. The cost assumes the principal is repaid at maturity.
findings.matters: The cost of EFS is a recurring revenue charge over two decades, so it affects the council's future budget capacity and the cost of its debt.
findings.figures: £83,000 annual cost per £1m EFS; 20 years; £8.8m annual cost on a £106.0m cumulative shortfall
findings.quote: at current rates each £1m of EFS used will add £83,000 to revenue costs annually for the next 20 years.

findings.headline: External loans were £1.2bn at 31 March 2026, up from £993m at 31 March 2025.
findings.detail: The auditor says the borrowing is at a record high, and that a large ongoing capital programme is to be financed with new borrowing, which is contributing to higher interest payable.
findings.matters: A council whose external borrowing has risen by about £233m in a year, and plans more, is directly relevant to lenders and to peers planning their own capital programmes.
findings.figures: £1.2bn external loans at 31 March 2026; £993m at 31 March 2025; year-end borrowings £1,226m
findings.quote: The Council’s external borrowing is at a record high, with loans of £1.2bn as of 31 March 2026

findings.headline: £10.1m was drawn unplanned from General Fund earmarked reserves in 2025/26, and the un-earmarked General Fund reserve was £15.2m.
findings.detail: The auditor says the un-earmarked reserve is less than 5% of the annual budget, and that the overall General Fund reserve remained consistent year on year despite the unplanned drawdown. The council also released £1.4m of unallocated grant reserves.
findings.matters: A drawdown from earmarked reserves to close a year's position reduces the council's buffer against future shocks, which a lender or peer would weigh.
findings.figures: £10.1m unplanned drawdown from earmarked reserves; £15.2m un-earmarked General Fund reserve; under 5% of annual budget; £1.4m released grant reserves; General Fund reserves £52.3m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: an unplanned drawdown of £10.1m from the General Fund earmarked reserves

findings.headline: Final 2025/26 EFS drawdown was £40.6m, against £37m in the approved budget.
findings.detail: MHCLG approved up to £54m of EFS in February 2026. The final drawdown was lower because of the improved position from Q3 to Q4 and an unplanned drawdown from earmarked reserves. The 2024/25 outturn also relied on £10m of EFS.
findings.matters: EFS is capitalisation funding that the council must repay, so its size and drawdown determine the council's repayment cost and debt position.
findings.figures: £40.6m final drawdown; £37m agreed in the approved budget; £54m approved ceiling; £3.6m increase; £10m used for 2024/25 outturn
findings.quote: ultimately the final drawdown of EFS was £40.6m

findings.headline: The 2025/26 overspend forecast fell from £34.1m at Q1 to £3.6m at year end, after £23.4m at Q2 and £19.4m at Q3.
findings.detail: The auditor attributes the year-end improvement mainly to corporately held budgets (£7.4m) and Adults (£6.4m). It describes the large swings in forecast delivery between quarters as not indicating a stable cost management environment.
findings.matters: A movement of £30.5m between Q1 and year end shows how volatile in-year forecasts can be, which matters to any finance director relying on quarterly monitoring.
findings.figures: Q1 forecast overspend £34.1m; Q2 £23.4m; Q3 £19.4m; year-end £3.6m; corporate budgets improvement £7.4m; Adults improvement £6.4m
findings.quote: a significantly improved position of a £3.6m overspend as of the year end.

findings.headline: Savings delivered in 2025/26 were £19.1m (65%) against a £29.3m target, a £10.2m shortfall.
findings.detail: The auditor notes that the 65% achievement rate is in line with 2024/25 (63%). It also notes progress in the gross value of savings delivered, which rose almost 50% year on year. The £13.4m of cross-cutting savings were intended to be allocated to services before 1 April 2025, but £5.7m remained unallocated during the year.
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls against a large target are the main driver of the auditor's financial sustainability finding, and other councils face the same cross-cutting savings structure.
findings.figures: £29.3m target; £19.1m (65%) delivered; £10.2m shortfall; £13.4m cross-cutting savings; £5.7m unallocated; gross savings delivered up almost 50%
findings.quote: The final position for 2025/26 was £19.1m (65%) of savings delivered against the £29.3m target – a £10.2m shortfall.

findings.headline: KPMG has made one Schedule 7 statutory recommendation, linked to a 2026/27 budget approved with a planned shortfall, and two non-statutory recommendations
findings.detail: The statutory recommendation escalates the previous value for money recommendations for greater visibility of management's progress. The 2026/27 budget was approved with a planned shortfall covered by Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), which the auditor links to the statutory recommendation.
findings.matters: A statutory recommendation is the strongest tool available to an auditor, and it arises from budget approval practice that other councils may share.
findings.figures: 1 statutory recommendation; 2 non-statutory recommendations
findings.quote: As at the date of this report, we have made 1 recommendation under Schedule 7 of the Act, alongside 2 non-statutory recommendations.

findings.headline: KPMG will issue a disclaimer of opinion on Haringey's 2025/26 financial statements by 29 January 2027.
findings.detail: The auditor says it has been unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the financial statements. Further details will be set out in the final Auditor's Annual Report. KPMG expects an unmodified opinion on the Haringey Pension Fund financial statements, subject to outstanding procedures.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, needs to know that the council's accounts are not being given an audit opinion on which they can rely.
findings.figures: Disclaimer of opinion by 29 January 2027
findings.quote: We will issue a disclaimer of opinion on the Council’s financial statements by 29 January 2027.

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: Children with Disabilities audit rated Limited: statutory assessments were not completed within timescales, with the Disabled Children's Team revenue budget at £1.8m for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The audit attributed delays to capacity pressures, competing operational priorities and the absence of a documented local process for monitoring and escalating overdue assessments. One priority 1 recommendation is due for implementation by January 2027.
findings.matters: Statutory assessment backlogs in a demand-led service carry both service and legal risk, and a finance director would weigh the cost of clearing the backlog against the rising cost of care packages.
findings.figures: £1.8m (2025/26 revenue budget); three recommendations, one priority 1
findings.quote: assessments were not completed within statutory timescales

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: Thirteen final internal audit reports issued in the quarter to August 2026: four rated Adequate and eight rated Limited.
findings.detail: The paper states that a number of control weaknesses were identified and that management accepted all recommendations. The Forvis Mazars programme delivered 130 days of work against 153 planned for the period to 31 August 2026, out of an annual plan of 723 days.
findings.matters: The ratio of Limited to Adequate ratings across a council's audit plan is the headline assurance measure a finance director or lender would use to judge control environment quality.
findings.figures: 13 final reports; four Adequate; eight Limited; 130 days delivered of 153 planned; 723-day annual plan
findings.quote: a total of 13 final internal audit reports were issued; four were assigned “Adequate” assurance, eight were assigned a “Limited” level of assurance

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: Commercially leased property compliance review rated Limited: 24 of 60 expected certificates were missing from a sample of ten Corporate Landlord managed properties.
findings.detail: The audit noted that the Council did not hold a central compliance monitoring system to evidence full health and safety compliance across the commercial estate. The paper records a 2024 audit of the same area also rated Limited, with recurring findings. Eleven recommendations were raised, two as priority 1, with implementation due by March 2028.
findings.matters: Repeat Limited ratings on the same property area, with a compliance gap that a lender or auditor would consider a contingent liability, are relevant to any council managing a large commercial portfolio.
findings.figures: 24 missing certificates out of 60; ten properties sampled; six statutory compliance areas; 11 recommendations, two priority 1; implementation by March 2028
findings.quote: found 24 missing certificates out of 60

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: Garage rent collection reached 95.46% year to date for weeks one to 30 of 2025/26, against a 99.50% target.
findings.detail: The paper records £413,929.63 collected against total charges of £433,617.40 for the period. The audit also found that garage management data is inaccurate or inconsistently reconciled across systems, with approximately 734 garages generating rental income and 700 void garages.
findings.matters: A gap between collected and due rent on a council-owned asset base, combined with unreliable records of which garages are let, bears on how completely rental income is identified and collected.
findings.figures: 95.46% (year-to-date collection rate); 99.50% (2025/26 target); £413,929.63 collected; £433,617.40 charged; approximately 734 garages let; 700 void garages
findings.quote: representing a year-to date collection rate of 95.46%

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: SEN transport audit rated Limited, with contracted services cost for the year projected at circa £5m as of December 2025.
findings.detail: The audit identified that onsite inspections of suppliers were not completed on a regular basis because the Contract Compliance Manager post was absent. The paper notes that demand for SEN transport has increased across the local government sector, with rising costs following growth in children with EHCPs.
findings.matters: Rising SEN transport demand and cost is a pressure reported across the sector, and a finance director at another council would want to know how a peer is controlling supplier oversight on a rising cost line.
findings.figures: circa £5m (projected contracted services cost for the year); six recommendations, one priority 1
findings.quote: with a projected contracted services cost for the year of circa £5m as of December 2025

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: Commissioning audit in Children's and Young People's Services rated Limited, as the Council-wide Commissioning Panel began operating in January 2026 for activity above £160k.
findings.detail: The audit found the Commissioning Framework, Contract Monitoring Framework and procurement coordination in place, and raised six recommendations including a standardised contract register and central storage of procurement documents. The paper links the work to the Commissioning Modernisation Programme approved in August 2025.
findings.matters: A council reorganising how it commissions a £600m annual spend, with a new approval threshold, is a governance change finance officers at other councils managing similar spend would compare against.
findings.figures: £600m (annual commissioned spend); £160k (Panel threshold); six recommendations, one priority 1
findings.quote: now reviews and approves all commissioning activity above £160k

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: Outstanding adult social care debt from client contributions is over £16m, with 473 clients not yet financially assessed.
findings.detail: The audit noted an average of 178 days to complete financial assessments against a 28-day target and a cumulative weekly cost of over £200k for clients without an assessment. The paper says performance had not significantly improved despite previous initiatives.
findings.matters: Uncollected care contributions and delayed assessments affect the income that offsets adult social care spend, which is a recurring pressure for councils and a credit consideration for lenders.
findings.figures: over £16m (outstanding ASC debt); 473 clients; 178 average days to complete assessments; 28-day target; over £200k cumulative weekly cost
findings.quote: There were 473 clients that had not had a financial assessment, with a cumulative weekly cost of over £200k.

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: Essential spend approvals under the Spend Control Panel, introduced from 12 March 2026 for spend over £1,000, rated Limited: a Spend Control Panel e-form was not held for most transactions tested.
findings.detail: The audit found the essential spend criteria were well defined, but the Spend Control Panel process has not been consistently embedded across directorates. The paper states that the control was introduced following the receipt of Exceptional Financial Support from the Government.
findings.matters: A council under Exceptional Financial Support introducing spending controls is a governance measure other finance directors and lenders would track, and this audit shows the control not yet operating as designed.
findings.figures: over £1,000 (threshold); 12 March 2026 (go-live date); four recommendations, one priority 1
findings.quote: for the majority of transactions tested, a SCP e-form was not held

findings.paper_title: IA progress report Cover Qtr 1 202627 - covering report
findings.headline: Directorate-owned savings against a 2025/26 target of £29.297m: the audit found the full-year forecast shows a shortfall in several directorates, rated Limited.
findings.detail: The audit found evidence supporting the projected savings and monthly monitoring, but only a fraction of the target had been delivered at the time of the audit. The paper also notes that year-to-date savings were not accurately recorded in the Savings Tracker.
findings.matters: A savings shortfall against a stated target in a council under Exceptional Financial Support is directly relevant to the sustainability of its medium-term plan, both for its own finance team and for peers and lenders assessing the same pressure.
findings.figures: £29.297 million (2025/26 target); three recommendations, one priority 1
findings.quote: against a 2025/26 target of £29.297 million

findings.headline: SEN Transport audit records increased costs, attributed to rising demand for SEN transport provision.
findings.detail: The audit rationale says the service has undergone substantial modifications since 2021 and that management commissioned the review to test whether the procedures introduced are working as intended. The highest priority finding is that onsite inspections of suppliers were not completed on a regular basis, with the absence of the Contract Compliance Manager given as the root cause.
findings.matters: Rising demand driving up cost in a statutory service is a pressure that other councils' finance officers budgeting for SEN transport would recognise.
findings.figures: Priority 1 (High) 1, Priority 2 (Medium) 4, Priority 3 (Low) 1; Priority 1 completion 31 October 2026; overall completion 30 April 2027
findings.quote: the service is facing increased costs, primarily attributed to rising demand for SEN transport provision

findings.headline: Repairs and Maintenance of Commercially Leased Property audit finds 24 of 60 sampled statutory certificates missing across ten Corporate Landlord properties.
findings.detail: The report says the council lacked a central compliance monitoring system for its commercial estate and that the Commercial Property Team does not hold statutory certificates for some properties. Responsibilities for keeping statutory compliance documents were unclear between Corporate Landlord and the Commercial Property Team. Ten leases were found to set out health and safety responsibilities.
findings.matters: Missing statutory compliance certificates on a commercial portfolio affects the council's ability to evidence that its property income and assets meet legal requirements.
findings.figures: 24 of 60 certificates missing across 6 statutory compliance areas; Priority 1 (High) 2, Priority 2 (Medium) 9; Priority 1 completion 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Sample review of ten Corporate Landlord managed properties found 24 missing certificates out of 60

findings.headline: Garage voids "not effectively monitored, prioritised, or managed"; 2 High, 2 Medium, 4 Low priority; Priority 1 due 31 December 2026
findings.detail: The report says garage voids have been deprioritised relative to housing repairs activity, and that garage management data is split across multiple teams and systems without clear ownership. It identifies a risk that rental income is not fully identified and that garages are incorrectly recorded as occupied.
findings.matters: Garage rental is a small but recurring income stream, and inaccurate void data means the income forecast built on it may not reflect what is actually let.
findings.figures: Priority 1 (High) 2, Priority 2 (Medium) 2, Priority 3 (Low) 4; Priority 1 completion 31 December 2026
findings.quote: Garage voids not effectively monitored, prioritised, or managed.

findings.headline: Financial Assessments audit finds assessments not completed within the 28-day target, with a backlog cited as the cause.
findings.detail: The review sampled ten financial assessments, all of which had supporting evidence obtained and reviewed, and testing confirmed annual uplift letters were issued for all 12 samples. The highest priority finding is delays against the 28-day target, with prioritising the longstanding backlog given as the root cause.
findings.matters: Timeliness of client contribution assessments affects when the council collects care income, which is relevant to income forecasting in adult social care.
findings.figures: 28-day assessment target; Priority 1 (High) 1, Priority 2 (Medium) 3; overall completion 31 January 2027
findings.quote: Financial assessments were not consistently completed in a timely manner.

findings.headline: Management responses to draft internal audit reports average 18 days against a 10 working day target.
findings.detail: The report says management response times continue to exceed the expected 10 working days from the draft report being issued. It asks the Audit Committee to seek assurance on overdue 2025/26 responses and request a recovery plan. Draft reports on Corporate Health & Safety in Housing and Asbestos Management in Housing Stock remain outstanding.
findings.matters: Delays in management responses leave audit findings unresolved, which affects how quickly control weaknesses in finance and property are addressed.
findings.figures: 18 days average management response against a target of 10 working days; draft report issued within 13.8 days average against a 15 working day target
findings.quote: the management responses times continue to exceed the expectations of 10 working days from the draft report being issued

findings.headline: Efficient and Effective use of Temporary Accommodation audit reassessed from Limited to Adequate assurance after management action.
findings.detail: The report says the audit was initially assigned Limited assurance, but after prompt management action implemented appropriate controls, the assurance was reviewed and raised to Adequate. The audit is one of the 2025/26 reviews finalised in the period.
findings.matters: A limited opinion lifted to adequate after control changes is a clear example of a council recovering an audit weakness, which other finance officers facing similar pressures would want to see.
findings.figures: Assurance reassessed from Limited to Adequate; Priority 1 (High) 1, Priority 2 (Medium) 1, total 2 findings
findings.quote: the assurance was reviewed and an “Adequate” level of assurance assigned

findings.headline: Audit of project management of non-corporate savings finds year-to-date savings not accurately recorded in the Savings Tracker.
findings.detail: The report says the sample of five savings plans had sufficient evidence to support projected savings, were monitored monthly, and had issues escalated to Corporate Finance. The highest priority finding is inaccurate year-to-date recording, with the root cause given as a lack of clear guidance on how savings should be reported.
findings.matters: How savings delivery is recorded determines whether a council's medium-term plan can be tracked against actual delivery, which is central to the savings plans underpinning its budget.
findings.figures: 5 savings plans in the sample; Priority 1 (High) 1, Priority 2 (Medium) 1, Priority 3 (Low) 1; Priority 1 completion 'Complete'; overall completion 30 September 2026
findings.quote: Year to Date Savings were not accurately recorded

findings.headline: Audit of the essential spend approval process finds no Spend Control Panel e-form held for 23 of 25 sampled transactions over £1,000 (92%).
findings.detail: The review follows the council's recently introduced process requiring directors to approve essential spend over £1,000, which the report links to Exceptional Financial Support from the Government. The root cause given is that the Spend Control Panel process has not been consistently embedded across directorates, with limited impact for non-compliance.
findings.matters: Under exceptional financial support, approval of essential spend is a key control on the council's in-year spending, and a finance director at another council would want to know how far such a process holds in practice.
findings.figures: 23 of 25 sampled transactions (92%) with no Spend Control Panel e-form; Priority 1 (High) 1, Priority 2 (Medium) 2, Priority 3 (Low) 1; Priority 1 completion 30 September 2026
findings.quote: in 23 cases (92%), no SCP e-form was held

findings.headline: Eight of the 13 (62%) assurance-related reports finalised since the last committee carry Limited assurance opinions.
findings.detail: The report says the volume of limited opinions represents control failures across a number of Council departments, with recurring themes across finance, property, commissioning and service management. It states the pattern may affect the annual Head of Internal Audit opinion.
findings.matters: A run of limited opinions across finance and property is the kind of signal that bears on the annual head of internal audit opinion and on how far the council's controls can be relied on.
findings.figures: 8 of 13 (62%) assurance-related reports with limited assurance; 2026/27 plan RAG status 'On Track'
findings.quote: eight of the 13 (62%) assurance-related reports have been limited

findings.paper_title: Appendix1 Treasury Management Update Report Q2 2026.27 V1 (1)
findings.headline: The average credit score of the Council's in-house investments moved from 4.95 at 31.03.2026 to 4.01 at 30.09.2026, on Arlingclose's benchmarking
findings.detail: The paper reports that Arlingclose's benchmarking shows an improvement in the credit ratings and score of the Council's investments over the period. The Council's score is better than the similar-authority average of 4.72 and the all-authority average of 4.58. The scale runs from AAA = 1 to D = 26, and the aim is a score of 7 or lower.
findings.matters: A lower score means higher credit quality of the cash held, which is relevant to any counterparty exposure a lender or finance director assesses.
findings.figures: Credit score 4.95 (31.03.26) to 4.01 (30.09.26); similar local authorities 4.72; all local authorities 4.58; portfolio average credit score A+, 4.68 against a target of 6.0 or lower

findings.paper_title: Appendix1 Treasury Management Update Report Q2 2026.27 V1 (1)

findings.headline: Pension fund secondary contribution rate set at 2.8% for next three years
findings.detail: The triennial actuarial valuation sets the employer secondary contribution rate at 2.8% for the whole fund for the next three years. Haringey Council comprises the majority of the fund and acts as a stabilising employer. This rate-setting approach is common across other Local Government Pension Funds.
findings.matters: The secondary rate directly affects the council's budget requirements for pension contributions and signals the fund's funding position; a stable rate indicates the fund is in reasonable health relative to liabilities.

findings.headline: Actual inflation in April 2026 of 3.8% exceeded the 3.3% assumption in the March 2025 valuation
findings.detail: Observed inflation has been higher than anticipated, resulting in LGPS pension increases of 3.8% in April 2026 against the 3.3% assumption embedded in the 2025 valuation. This increases the present value of promised pension liabilities. The actuary notes this inflation trajectory requires monitoring for assumption revisions.
findings.matters: Higher inflation drives up the cost of pension benefits and creates upward pressure on funding position; indicates that assumption revisions may be required at the next valuation in 2028

findings.headline: 79% of fund assets transitioned to London CIV pooling arrangement, below the March 2026 government target for full transfer
findings.detail: £1.671bn of £2.111bn net assets (79%) had transferred to the London Collective Investment Vehicle by year-end. Government 'Fit for the Future' guidance (May 2025) set expectation of 'transferring all assets by March 2026'. Asset pooling generated net savings of £1.288m to the fund in 2025/26 after accounting for all LCIV charges.
findings.matters: Incomplete asset pooling creates regulatory compliance uncertainty, though partially offset by demonstrated cost savings of £1.3m annually from pooling activity
findings.figures: Assets in LCIV: £1.671bn of £2.111bn (79%); net savings 2025/26: £1.288m after LCIV charges
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Fund had transitioned £1.671 billion, representing 79% of its assets, into LCIV. In 2025/26, the net saving to the Fund for the year was £1.288million.

findings.headline: Administration costs per member rose 6.7% to £53.80, with staffing headcount up and vacancy rate at 23%

findings.matters: Rising per-member costs combined with elevated vacancy rate signal labour market pressures and capacity constraints that could affect administration service quality
findings.quote: Administration costs per member £53.80; Administration FTEs 13.0; Staff vacancy rate as % 23

findings.headline: Pension benefits paid exceeded contributions received by £6.7m, a structural position reflecting fund maturity
findings.detail: Benefits of £74.5m paid in 2025/26 exceeded contributions of £67.8m by £6.7m. This gap, covered by investment income in the year, reflects declining active membership relative to pensioners and deferred members. Benefits have exceeded contributions for several years.
findings.matters: Structural maturity makes the fund increasingly dependent on investment returns to fund benefit payments, reducing tolerance for sustained underperformance
findings.figures: Benefits paid £74.5m; contributions £67.8m; shortfall £6.7m
findings.quote: Contributions have grown at a slower pace than benefits paid, reflecting the increasing maturity of the Fund's membership profile. Benefits have exceeded contributions for several years, with the shortfall covered by investment income.

findings.headline: Fund valued at 139% of liabilities at 31 March 2025, with actuarial statement indicating likely strengthening since
findings.detail: Assets of £1,933m at the most recent actuarial valuation were valued at 139% of pension liabilities. The fund actuary stated: 'Overall, we estimate that the funding position is likely to be stronger than at the previous formal valuation at 31 March 2025.' Employer contribution rates are locked in through March 2029. Next valuation is at 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: Strong funding position removes solvency risk, confirms scheme sustainability, and protects participating employers from unexpected contribution rises
findings.figures: Assets £1,933m at 31 March 2025; funding level 139% of liabilities
findings.quote: The fund's assets, which at 31 March 2025 were valued at £1,933 million, were sufficient to meet 139% of the liabilities (i.e. the present value of promised retirement benefits) accrued up to that date.

findings.detail: One-year returns of 9.5% fell 90 basis points short of the 10.4% benchmark. Three-year returns of 7.7% trailed the 9.4% benchmark by 170bp. Five-year returns of 5.7% lagged the 6.8% benchmark by 110bp. The actuarial statement attributes recent volatility to US tariff increases and Middle East conflict.
findings.matters: Persistent underperformance against benchmarks is material to long-term fund sustainability, especially given the fund's mature membership profile where benefits increasingly exceed contributions

findings.detail: The audit has identified zero significant control deficiencies in the pension fund's control environment. No significant control deficiencies existed in the prior year.
findings.matters: The absence of significant control deficiencies provides positive assurance on the design and operating effectiveness of the fund's key internal controls, though the continuing journal posting weakness limits the overall control environment assessment.

findings.figures: No reportable misstatements; no fraud indicators identified
findings.quote: We found no reportable misstatements or indicators of fraud in our testing. We expect to issue an unmodified Auditor's Report

findings.headline: £5.96m adjustment made to investment valuations; updated valuations not available at year-end closedown
findings.detail: The auditors identified and management corrected a misstatement of £5.96m relating to Level 3 investments (unquoted and illiquid assets where valuations depend on fund managers' information). Updated valuations were not available when the pension fund closed its accounts on 31 March 2026 and were only received from fund managers after year-end. The audit adjustment updated the investment balance to reflect these subsequent valuations. Level 3 investments are a significant portion of the fund's holdings.
findings.matters: A material post-year-end adjustment to investment valuations indicates the pension fund's year-end financial position was incomplete and that its valuation processes for complex illiquid assets do not conclude by the accounting close date.
findings.figures: £5.96m adjustment; investments represent 99.89% of total pension fund assets
findings.quote: Due to the timing of the funds' valuation processes, updated valuations were not available at the Fund's year-end closedown. The audit adjustment updates the investment balance to reflect the subsequent valuations received from the fund managers after the year end.

findings.headline: Segregation of duties control deficiency on manual journal posting recurs from prior year; auditors cannot rely on management's informal compensating control
findings.detail: The audit identifies that there are no segregation of duties controls when posting manual journals directly to the ledger, and journals below £40,000 do not require approval by another person. This deficiency was also raised in the prior year and remains unresolved. Management implemented a compensating control to review journals impacting balance sheet movements, but auditors cannot rely on this as it remains informal in nature and lacks formal status. Management acknowledges the issue and commits to implement a 'park and post' approach for all journals by April 2027.
findings.matters: A recurring control weakness over journal posting creates fraud risk and financial statement accuracy risk; the informality of compensating controls means the underlying deficiency remains unmitigated despite prior-year notification.
findings.figures: Journals below £40,000 exempt from approval requirement; implementation deadline April 2027
findings.quote: We identified that there are no segregation of duties controls when posting manual journals directly to the ledger. findings.detail: A rebalancing plan (reviewed August 2026, presented to Investment and Governance Working Group September 2026) was agreed to deploy part of the fund's cash holdings. findings.figures: Last quarter 6.1% actual vs 7.1% benchmark; one year 12.7% vs 14.4%; three years 9.7% vs 12.3%; five years 6.0% vs 7.7%

findings.headline: Children's services forecast £3.1m overspend driven by 9% growth in residential care placement costs against 3-3.5% inflation assumed at budget-setting.
findings.detail: Children's Services overspend is £3.1m at Q1. Weekly costs for children in residential care have risen from £196k (April 2026) to £233k (June 2026), an increase of £37k per week or £1.9m annualised. Top 25 placements alone have increased from £155.5k per week to £200.9k per week (£2.36m annualised increase). Council notes: 'increase in complexity and higher unit costs, for placements that require a high level of supervision and care, is causing the additional pressure in demand-led services, this is often difficult to predict.'
findings.matters: Placement cost inflation running at 9% (three times assumed rate) is a core service pressure with no discretionary offset. Complexity is rising; the service cannot reduce numbers without statutory/reputational consequence. This is a multi-year pressure.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves of £52m are lower than average for a council of Haringey's size; General Fund Reserve of £15.1m will not be used to mitigate in-year overspend.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspending by £176m (24% slippage) with major schemes including regeneration and HRA acquisitions delayed.
findings.detail: Q1 forecast capital spend is £545.2m against £721.4m budget (75.6% of budget). General Fund forecast £234.4m against £344.4m budget; HRA forecast £310.7m against £376.9m budget. Major variances include: Children's £14.8m underspend (6 projects delayed through feasibility and complexity issues); Culture £46.9m underspend (Shaping Tottenham, Shaping Wood Green, High Road West slipped); HRA £66.2m underspend (acquisitions slowed, major works mobilising). Paper notes 'trend of high levels of slippage has continued into current year' and flags that schemes without business case, delivery plan and assurance will be placed into pipeline.
findings.matters: Capital slippage means either planned delivery is overoptimistic, or conditions preventing delivery are not forecast at budget-setting. Either way, a lender seeing a council underspend capital by 24% at Q1 with three-quarters of the year to run faces uncertainty on both project timeline and borrowing requirement.
findings.figures: £545.2m forecast spend against £721.4m budget; £176.2m underspend; General Fund £234.4m vs £344.4m; HRA £310.7m vs £376.9m
findings.quote: It should be noted that the trend of high levels of slippage has continued into the current year. The review of the capital programme is underway as part of the preparation for the 2027/28 capital programme that will be published in March 2027. Any scheme without an approved business case, clear delivery plan and assurance on delivery will be placed into the pipeline.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecasting £3.478m deficit, driven by £10.2m income under-recovery from void properties and temporary accommodation pressures.
findings.detail: HRA is £3.5m in deficit. Main issue is £10.2m under-recovery of income from void properties, where council budgeted 2% void rate but is experiencing higher voids from decant programmes, stock turnover and acquisitions. Improvement plan in place aiming to increase void turnaround from September 2026, to be monitored through quarterly reports. Temporary accommodation within HRA contributing £2.9m overspend separately.
findings.matters: Void losses represent cash not collected that was assumed in the business plan. A landlord authority with structural void issues has working capital problems; improvement plans are often slow to deliver, and the 2% void assumption may itself be unachievable.
findings.figures: £3.478m HRA deficit forecast; £10.213m net income under-recovery from voids; 2% void rate budgeted vs higher actual
findings.quote: There is a net under recovery of income of £10.213m mainly due to a forecast higher than budgeted level of void properties throughout the year. The income profile was adjusted for a 2% void rate for 2026/27 which represents a challenging target given levels of voids that arise through decant programmes, increased stock turnover and the acquisition programme

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit of £12.7m will remain at £3.3m even if government approves planned £9.3m SEND improvement payment.
findings.detail: DSG is forecasting £8.4m Q1 overspend, all from High Needs Block (SEND). Council has submitted SEND Improvement Plan seeking £9.4m payment which, if approved, would reduce accumulated deficit from £12.7m to £3.3m. Schools themselves in deficit: £7.7m at Q1, up from £4.1m at 2025/26 year-end. Council is working with schools on recovery plans 'which may lead to further academisation and/or closures.'
findings.matters: SEND deficits are structural (demand-led, statutory, not discretionary) and persist even with government support. Schools in deficit remain a contingent liability: council is ultimately responsible for their recovery and closure. A peer authority watching Haringey faces similar pressures.
findings.figures: £8.4m DSG overspend Q1; accumulated deficit £12.7m; potential government payment £9.4m; projected remaining deficit £3.3m; schools deficit £7.7m (Q1) up from £4.1m (year-end)
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) forecast at Quarter 1 stands at £8.4m overspend which is fully in relation to the High Needs Block... The number of schools in or facing deficits continues to rise. The 2025/26 outturn deficit for schools was £4.1m. However, at the end of quarter 1 this has increased to £7.7m.

findings.matters: Savings that fail across consecutive years cease to be credible as plans; they indicate either original overestimation, delivery failures, or both. A lender seeing a council unable to deliver its own cost-reduction programme for two years running faces elevated refinancing risk.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £84.3m now forecast insufficient; council warns that borrowing to cover the gap will add £86,000 per £1m annually for 20 years.
findings.detail: Council requires £84.3m government EFS to balance the 2026/27 budget. Paper states: 'there is a substantial risk that, if the current forecast overspend on services cannot be brought down significantly and an improvement on the delivery of savings before year end, the assumed use of £84.3m of Exceptional Financial Support will not be sufficient.' Each £1m of EFS borrowed at current rates will add £86,000 annual revenue cost for 20 years at maturity.
findings.matters: EFS is already a marker of financial distress; a council anticipating it will need even more EFS signals that government support is becoming structural to the authority's finances rather than temporary, and borrowing implications compound the problem.
findings.figures: £84.3m EFS in budget; £86,000 per £1m annual cost for 20 years if borrowed
findings.quote: there is a substantial risk that, if the current forecast overspend on services cannot be brought down significantly and an improvement on the delivery of savings before year end, the assumed use of £84.3m of Exceptional Financial Support will not be sufficient. This further increases the financial burden on the authority due to increased borrowing costs. At current rates each £1m of EFS used will add £86,000 to revenue costs each year for the next 20 years

findings.headline: External borrowing increased 23.6% in one year; HRA borrowing up 17.6%
findings.detail: Total external borrowing rose from £981.3m to £1,213.4m (£232.1m increase). The underlying Capital Financing Requirement increased from £1,418.9m to £1,565.0m. HRA CFR increased particularly sharply from £626.8m to £736.9m. This trajectory, combined with high interest rates, underpins the council's assessment that borrowing growth is unsustainable.
findings.matters: A 23.6% year-on-year increase in borrowing raises sustainability questions. When a council describes its own borrowing trajectory as 'not sustainable', it signals expected financial pressure ahead.
findings.quote: the Council held £1,213.4 million in loans on 31 March 2026, an increase of £232.1 million compared to 31 March 2025.

findings.headline: PFI and finance lease liabilities breach authorised prudential limit
findings.detail: PFI and finance lease balances reached £45.0m at year-end, breaching the authorised limit of £13.9m by £31.1m and the operational boundary of £12.7m. The council explicitly notes this as an exception to full compliance. This breach was also reported at Q3.
findings.matters: Exceeding prudential limits in a specific borrowing category reduces headroom and shows the council is operating outside its approved strategy. Persistent breaches may signal deteriorating financial discipline.
findings.figures: Actual £45.0m; Authorised Limit £13.9m (breach £31.1m); Operational Boundary £12.7m.
findings.quote: all treasury management activities carried out during the period complied fully with the principles in the Treasury Management Code and the Council's approved Treasury Management Strategy with the exception of lease levels in comparison to the Operational Boundary and Authorised Limit as detailed below, which was also reported in the Quarter 3 monitoring report earlier in the year.

findings.headline: £50m LOBO loans face refinancing demand within 12 months at materially higher rates
findings.detail: All £50m of Haringey's LOBO loans have call dates within April 2026. If lenders exercise these options, the council will need to refinance or repay. Current market rates for 10-year PWLB borrowing (5.72%) are substantially higher than the LOBO loans' current 4.73% rate.
findings.matters: This is an immediate refinancing obligation. If lenders call, the council faces significantly higher borrowing costs when refinancing at current rates, increasing annual debt service.
findings.figures: £50m LOBO loans at 4.73% weighted average rate. Next call dates: 10/04/2026. Current 10-year PWLB rate: 5.72%.
findings.quote: All LOBO loans the Council held at year end have call dates within the next 12 months.

findings.headline: Council reviewing capital programme to identify schemes that can be paused or slowed; external borrowing increased £232.1m to £1,213.4m
findings.detail: Haringey will review its capital programme during summer 2026 to identify schemes that can be paused or slowed. The council explicitly cites high interest rates, ongoing reliance on EFS, and unsustainable year-on-year borrowing increases as drivers. This represents a material shift in capital spending plans.
findings.matters: A council actively pausing capital schemes signals financial distress and indicates a deterioration in financial position. For lenders, this is a leading indicator of financial difficulty and reduced investment capacity.
findings.figures: External borrowing increased £232.1m to £1,213.4m in 2025/26. Capital Financing Requirement increased £146.1m to £1,565.0m.
findings.quote: the Council will be reviewing its capital programme to identify schemes that can be paused  / slowed down given that interest rates remain high , reliance on EFS remains high and forecast year on year increase on borrowing is not sustainable.

findings.headline: Council seeks to reduce reliance on Exceptional Financial Support through increased savings delivery
findings.detail: The statutory officer's finance comments note that acceptance of KPMG's recommendations and council actions is 'expected to increase the level of savings agreed by the Council for 2027/28 onwards, improve delivery of these savings and reduce future reliance on Exceptional Financial Support.' This indicates the council currently depends on emergency government funding to balance its budget.
findings.matters: Councils reliant on Exceptional Financial Support are in financial distress; reducing that reliance requires closing structural deficits through service cuts or transformation, which poses ongoing financial risk.
findings.figures: None specific on savings gaps or EFS amounts
findings.quote: The Statutory Recommendation and Non-Statutory Recommendations and the actions by the Council is expected to increase the level of savings agreed by the Council for 2027/28 onwards, improve delivery of these savings and reduce future reliance on Exceptional Financial Support

findings.paper_title: STATUTORY RECOMMENDATION IN ACCORDANCE WITH SCHEDULE 7 OF THE LOCAL AUDIT AND ACCOUNTABILITY ACT
findings.headline: Council established Member Finance Recovery Board with monthly savings progress reporting
findings.detail: Full Council approved a cross-party Member Finance Recovery Board chaired by the Chief Executive as an amendment to its response to KPMG's recommendations. The Corporate Director of Finance will provide monthly savings reports detailing progress on savings in the current year, with reports to begin within one month of the council's formal response.
findings.matters: Creation of a high-level recovery board with chief-executive-level oversight and monthly monitoring suggests the council acknowledges significant financial management weakness and is implementing additional governance controls over savings delivery.
findings.figures: First monthly report due within one month of 20 July 2026 decision; reports to continue until superseded by new arrangements in November 2026
findings.quote: the Corporate Director of Finance and Resources will provide this Board with monthly savings reports detailing the progress on savings in the current year

findings.paper_title: STATUTORY RECOMMENDATION IN ACCORDANCE WITH SCHEDULE 7 OF THE LOCAL AUDIT AND ACCOUNTABILITY ACT
findings.headline: External auditor issues Statutory Recommendation due to inadequate planned savings in 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: KPMG warned in its January 2026 annual report that it would issue a Statutory Recommendation if the 2026/27 budget lacked adequate planned savings to address the council's 'challenging financial position'. When the council approved the 2026/27 budget on 2 March 2026, KPMG issued the Statutory Recommendation on 18 May 2026.
findings.matters: Statutory Recommendations from external auditors are rare formal escalations indicating the auditor believes the council's financial sustainability is threatened; this signals serious budget-balancing problems to lenders and regulators.
findings.figures: Statutory Recommendation issued 18 May 2026; considered by Full Council 20 July 2026
findings.quote: we expect that we will consider it necessary to raise such a statutory recommendation in future, should the budget for 2026/27 be approved without an appropriate level of planned savings to address the Council's challenging financial position

findings.headline: Prior year audit identified data reliability problems with Beacon properties that prevented audit conclusion on Council Dwellings valuation; now specific audit focus
findings.detail: Auditors note unresolved data quality issues: 'Given known issues in the prior year with the reliability of information regarding Beacon properties which prevented our conclusion over Council Dwellings in 24/25, we will have a specific focus on this area during the audit.' This indicates systemic property data management weaknesses.
findings.matters: Council Dwellings typically represent a material asset on the balance sheet. If the council cannot reliably provide property valuation data, this creates both audit risk and potential balance sheet risk.
findings.figures: Data reliability issues prevent prior-year audit conclusion on Council Dwellings
findings.quote: Given known issues in the prior year with the reliability of information regarding Beacon properties which prevented our conclusion over Council Dwellings in 24/25, we will have a specific focus on this area during the audit

findings.headline: Adult Social Care has CQC 'Requires Improvement' finding and council lacks adequate financial forecasting and management of this spend
findings.detail: Auditors have identified a significant VFM risk: the council lacks adequate processes to forecast and manage Adult Social Care spend in light of the CQC's 'Requires Improvement' rating. There are also concerns about timely assessment and recovery of patient contributions.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is typically the largest council budget. A CQC 'Requires Improvement' finding signals service stress. Combined with poor forecasting controls, this creates material risk of budget overruns and demand-driven overspends.
findings.figures: CQC rating: Requires Improvement
findings.quote: the Council does not have adequate processes in place to ensure that Social Care spend is sufficiently forecast and managed in light of the 'Requires Improvement' CQC findings, or that financial contributions from patients are assessed and recovered in a timely manner.

findings.headline: Council's budget shortfall is escalating: £54m Exceptional Financial Support in 2025/26, but already forecasting £84m need for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council faced a forecasted overspend of £19m at Q3 2025/26, improved to £14m by Month 11. It received an additional £17m EFS in February 2026 (bringing total to £54m) to meet the shortfall. It is already forecasting it will require £84m EFS for 2026/27 to balance its budget.
findings.matters: EFS is non-recurring government support. The escalation from £54m to £84m shows the council's underlying budget position is worsening significantly, not improving. This raises questions about long-term financial sustainability and the ability to service debt.
findings.figures: £54m EFS in 2025/26, £84m EFS required for 2026/27; £19m Q3 overspend, reduced to £14m by Month 11
findings.quote: Furthermore, the Council has faced difficulties in delivering this budget, with a forecasted overspend of £19m as at Q3, subsequently improved to £14m as at Month 11... MHCLG has approved an additional Exceptional Finance Support (EFS) allocation of £17m (to £54m) to the Council in February 2026 to meet the budget shortfall... The Council is also forecasting a substantial budget shortfall for 26/27 which required an agreed £84m EFS allocation in 26/27 with MHCLG to reach a balanced position.

findings.headline: Council has had disclaimed audit opinions for three consecutive years (2022/23–2024/25) and is undergoing rebuilding assurance work to restore audit opinion
findings.detail: The council received a disclaimer of opinion from the predecessor auditor for three years through 2022/23, a disclaimer for 2023/24 issued on 28 February 2025, and a disclaimed opinion for 2024/25 issued on 26 February 2026. The auditors are now conducting a formal rebuilding assurance risk assessment as part of the national 'Rest and Recovery' programme.
findings.matters: Three consecutive years of disclaimed opinions signals the council has struggled to produce auditable financial statements. This is a fundamental issue for lenders assessing financial reliability and governance.
findings.figures: 3 consecutive years of disclaimed opinions
findings.quote: For Haringey London Borough Council, this had the impact of a disclaimer of opinion issued by your predecessor auditor for 3 financial years up to and including 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to you previously. For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimed opinion on 26 February 2026.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support has doubled to £84m, with financial sustainability plan incomplete
findings.detail: The council's reliance on EFS has increased dramatically from £37m in 2025/26 to £84m in 2026/27. findings.headline: Contracts and Procurement has been a persistent area of concern for five years with no resolution
findings.detail: Contracts and Procurement was assigned Limited Assurance and has been an ongoing problem since 2020/21. The latest audit (2025/26) found that operational issues from 2024 persist: inconsistent contract monitoring, weak documentation, limited performance reporting, and unclear responsibilities. The audit attributed these to lack of corporate contract management framework, insufficient training, and fragmented systems, with missing signed contracts and poor configuration of the Contract Register.
findings.matters: Weak contract management exposes the council to supplier disputes, price overruns, poor service delivery, and potential legal liability. For a council under financial stress, uncontrolled contract performance is a material risk to both cost and service continuity.
findings.figures: None quantified; audit identified missing signed contracts and poor contract monitoring across multiple services.

findings.detail: The Head of Audit Opinion on Internal Controls is 'Limited Assurance', meaning significant weaknesses exist in governance, risk management, and control such that the system could be or could become inadequate and ineffective. The opinion specifically cites the council's continued reliance on Exceptional Financial Support and failure to deliver savings to balance budgets.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance on internal controls is a red flag for any lender. It means the council cannot reliably prevent, detect, or correct errors in financial management or service delivery. This undermines confidence in reported financial positions and forecast accuracy.
findings.figures: None provided; Limited Assurance rating applies council-wide to financial controls, operational controls, and compliance controls.
findings.quote: Internal Control Opinion – "Limited Assurance", based on effectiveness of financial controls, operational controls, compliance controls and key service controls

findings.headline: Savings delivery programme assigned 'Nil Assurance'—the lowest possible rating
findings.detail: Internal audit gave the council's Governance over Delivery of Savings a Nil Assurance rating. The audit found the council was not on track to meet its 2025/26 savings target, had insufficient documented evidence of regular review and robust challenge of progress, and lacked robust monitoring mechanisms and accountability structures. Monthly savings updates were not properly scrutinised and accountability was fragmented across departments.
findings.matters: Nil Assurance means the auditor has no confidence in the control framework. For a council under financial pressure relying on savings delivery, this indicates a material risk that planned financial improvements will not materialise.
findings.figures: Council was targeting unspecified savings for 2025/26 but audit found insufficient tracking and accountability.
findings.quote: the Council was not on track to meet its savings target for 2025/26 and there was insufficient documented evidence of regular review and robust challenge regarding progress against savings plan targets. The audit also noted the lack of robust monitoring mechanisms and accountability structures to scrutinise monthly savings updates

This is a statutory recommendation—the most serious form of audit finding.
findings.matters: A statutory recommendation signals that external auditors believe the council cannot deliver its current financial plan. This is a material credit risk and may trigger government intervention.
